analysis.one_liner: Bans courts from enforcing settlement secrecy deals that hide public health and safety hazards.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past its first day in the Senate: referred to the Judiciary Committee on May 12, 2014, it drew no cosponsors, never got a hearing or vote, and died when the Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have stopped federal courts from enforcing settlement deals in civil lawsuits that gag people from talking about dangers to public health or safety. When a case alleged such a hazard, companies could no longer require secrecy about the hazard, the evidence, or the settlement terms, and no settlement could block someone from reporting the problem to a safety regulator. Courts could still approve secrecy in narrow cases where a real confidentiality interest outweighed the public's interest in knowing, and personal privacy like medical records would stay protected.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone who could be exposed to a hidden hazard — consumers, workers, patients, and neighbors of polluting facilities — would benefit. When a lawsuit alleges a danger to public safety or health, the bill would stop courts from enforcing settlement clauses that gag the parties from discussing the hazard, the evidence, or the settlement terms (other than the dollar amount). It would also bar any settlement term that stops a party from reporting the hazard to a federal or state regulator or law-enforcement agency, so regulators could learn about dangers that today are settled away in secret [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers, workers, and patients exposed to hazards

how_it_helps.text: In any lawsuit where a pleading alleges a hazard to public safety or health, courts could not enforce settlement terms that prohibit a party from disclosing that the settlement happened, the settlement terms (other than the money paid), the evidence in the case, or the hazard itself [S2] [S3].

No court could approve any settlement provision that restricts a party from disclosing hazard information to a federal or state agency with law-enforcement or regulatory authority over the activity — closing the channel through which known dangers currently go unreported to regulators [S2] [S3].

The bill still protects genuine privacy: courts could keep secrecy for specific and substantial confidentiality interests, personal financial or medical information gets a presumption of protection, and courts could redact agreements to balance personal privacy against public awareness [S2] [S3].
A general interest in settling disputes — the usual rationale for sealing everything — would explicitly not count as a reason to keep hazard information secret [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Companies facing lawsuits over alleged safety or health hazards — product makers, drug companies, chemical firms — and their insurers would lose their ability to buy silence as part of a settlement. They could no longer rely on courts to enforce agreements that bar a plaintiff from ever telling regulators or the public about the hazard, which would make settling such cases harder and more expensive for them [S2] [S3].

drawbacks.text: Settlements exist partly to end disputes quickly; if secrecy clauses become unenforceable in hazard cases, some companies may fight longer instead of settling, delaying compensation to the very people the bill aims to protect [S2].

Some plaintiffs genuinely want confidentiality — for personal privacy, reputation, or negotiating leverage — and a default rule against secrecy could make some defendants refuse to settle at all rather than accept public disclosure [S2].

The bill adds a new layer of court proceedings: parties would litigate motions to balance confidentiality against public awareness in every hazard-related settlement, adding time and cost to the process [S2] [S3].
Courts already have inherent authority to refuse to enforce overbroad sealing orders, so critics would argue the bill solves a problem judges could address case by case [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and specific: known hazards — defective products, contaminated sites, dangerous drugs — stay hidden today because settlement gag clauses are routinely enforced, and the public and regulators never learn about them until someone else gets hurt. The bill carved out genuine privacy (medical and financial records get a presumption of protection) and let courts approve secrecy for real, specific interests, which answers the fairness objection. The honest cost is that settlements in hazard cases could become harder and slower to reach, and some cases would go to trial instead, delaying money for injured plaintiffs. On balance the public-safety gain outweighs that cost, which is why the bill's failure to even get a hearing leaves the status quo — secret settlements about known dangers — fully intact.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and never came back out; it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the Senate on May 12, 2014, and referred to the Judiciary Committee the same day [S5].
No cosponsors joined the bill during its entire life [S4].
The Judiciary Committee never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote, and the bill died when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015 [S5].
The bill was one of several secrecy-in-settlement proposals introduced that year amid public attention to hidden defects and safety hazards, but it received no committee action [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies facing safety-related lawsuits and their insurers are better off, because the existing practice of enforcing broad settlement secrecy agreements was left untouched. Members of the public injured by undisclosed hazards gained nothing.

for.name: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse
for.role: U.S. Senator from Rhode Island and bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks; it was read twice and referred to the Judiciary Committee

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral but took no further action — no hearings, markup, or floor vote — so it died at the end of the Congress

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the bill had a single Democratic sponsor, no cosponsors of either party, and died in committee, so no partisan split can be measured.

industries.industry: Product, drug, and chemical manufacturers facing liability suits
industries.note: These companies regularly use confidential settlements to keep hazard allegations out of public view and away from regulators, which prevents future customers and workers from learning about known dangers. The bill would take that option away whenever a lawsuit alleges a public safety or health hazard.
Insurers price and settle liability claims, and secrecy clauses are part of their settlement toolkit; restricting them raises expected settlement costs and litigation exposure for liability insurers.
